title: Commerce City
name: Commerce City
metaDescription: Commerce City 1031 exchange coordination for warehouse and rail-served industrial property along I-270 and I-76, where reverse exchanges and environmental review matter.

sections.html: Commerce City runs on industrial land, not retail charm. The Suncor refinery, the rail yards, and the warehouse space along I-270 and I-76 are the real story here, and every exchange I coordinate in this submarket starts with that fact. A buyer expecting a polished suburban office park is looking in the wrong part of the metro.

sections.heading: An Industrial Market With a Refinery in the Middle of It
sections.html: Commerce City's industrial base is genuinely industrial, refining, rail, distribution, not the light flex space that gets called industrial in some suburbs. That gives owners here real cash flow from tenants who need this specific kind of access and zoning, but it also means environmental history is a bigger diligence item than almost anywhere else in the metro, and a buyer coming from a cleaner suburban market needs to adjust expectations accordingly. Rail access in particular is not something every industrial suburb in the metro can offer, and tenants who depend on it will pay a premium to be here rather than somewhere with truck-only access. That premium has held even as speculative industrial construction has picked up elsewhere in the metro, since new suburban parks further out rarely come with a rail spur already in place, and adding one after the fact is rarely realistic given the cost and the railroad's own lengthy approval process.

sections.heading: What's Moving Through Exchanges
sections.html:
Warehouse and distribution space along the I-270 and I-76 corridors makes up most of the exchange volume, much of it leased to logistics and building-materials tenants. Land near the National Western Center has picked up interest as that campus continues to develop. Some retail exists to serve the industrial workforce, but it's a small share of the market. Rail-served parcels command a premium over trucking-only sites for tenants who depend on freight volume, and that premium shows up directly in asking price. Categories worth tracking:

  • Warehouse and distribution space along I-270 and I-76
  • Rail-served industrial land near the refinery and rail yards
  • Land near the National Western Center
  • Service retail catering to the industrial workforce
  • DST interests for owners exiting hands-on industrial management

sections.heading: Reverse Exchanges Fit This Market
sections.html: Good industrial product along I-270 gets bought fast, sometimes faster than a seller can close their relinquished property. That timing mismatch is exactly what a reverse exchange solves, letting a buyer secure the replacement property first through an exchange accommodation titleholder, then sell the relinquished property within the 180-day window. I bring up the reverse structure early with any Commerce City buyer worried about losing a good warehouse to a faster-moving competitor.

sections.heading: Environmental Diligence Isn't Optional Here
sections.html: Given the refinery, rail history, and decades of industrial use, a Phase I environmental report is the minimum, and a Phase II follows if the Phase I flags anything. Skipping this step to save time is the single most expensive mistake I've watched a Commerce City buyer make, since remediation costs discovered after closing don't care about your exchange deadline. Prior use records from the rail yards specifically deserve extra attention on any parcel near the tracks, since old fuel storage and cleaning operations from decades past don't always show up in a routine title search or a quick database pull.

sections.heading: Coordinating a Deal With Real Environmental Risk
sections.html: The qualified intermediary, environmental consultant, and lender all need to be talking to each other before the 45-day identification deadline, not after. A lender who gets surprised by a Phase II report mid-process can delay or kill the financing entirely, and that delay puts the whole exchange timeline at risk. I schedule the environmental consultant's initial review the same week the identification list is drafted, not after, so nobody is waiting on a report they should have ordered weeks earlier.

faqs.q: Why do reverse exchanges come up so often in Commerce City?
faqs.a: Good warehouse and distribution space along I-270 and I-76 moves fast, sometimes faster than a seller can close their relinquished property. A reverse exchange lets a buyer secure the replacement first through an accommodation titleholder, then sell within the 180-day window, which removes the pressure of losing a good building to a faster buyer.

faqs.q: Is a Phase I environmental report really necessary for every Commerce City deal?
faqs.a: Yes. Decades of refinery, rail, and industrial use make environmental history a real risk here, and skipping this diligence step to save time has been the most expensive mistake I've seen buyers make in this submarket. Parcels near the rail yards deserve especially close review.

faqs.q: What happens if a Phase II report is needed after I've already started my exchange?
faqs.a: It can delay financing and put pressure on the 180-day deadline, which is why the qualified intermediary, environmental consultant, and lender should be coordinating before the 45-day identification period ends, not after a problem surfaces mid-process.

faqs.q: Is land near the National Western Center a good 1031 replacement?
faqs.a: Interest has grown as that campus develops further, but confirm current zoning and any planned infrastructure changes before treating future development potential as certain value today.

faqs.q: Can 1031 Exchange Denver arrange my exchange accommodation titleholder for a reverse exchange?
faqs.a: No. This service coordinates scheduling and communication among the investor's team. The exchange accommodation titleholder and qualified intermediary are independent parties the investor engages directly, based on their CPA's and tax attorney's guidance, well before any reverse structure gets set up.
